mappings.note: POOR FIT, same hole as V49 and the widest version of it: iodine in thyroid medicine, uranium in energy. Curriculum 82 has no outcome about applications of anything, so only CG5's cross-curricular linkage reaches it. LO-3 is withheld deliberately - no property or definition of an isotope is graded, only what it is used for.

Two asks: name the relation (LO-3's isotope clause) and explain identical chemistry by valence electrons (LO-3 again), with the relation having to be read off three supplied diagrams first - LO-5's interpretation clause. Same treatment as O22; V47 and V50, which supply no data, get LO-3 alone.

PARTIAL FIT on one of its three axes. Charge and location are exactly LO-1 ('based on their charge, and position in the atom'), but relative MASS is not in LO-1 and is not in any other outcome either - the same gap recorded at V35 and S82.

Two clean halves: writing A and Z around the symbol is the international notation convention (LO-6), and the isobar verdict is LO-3. This is the split I use throughout - LO-6 for how a quantity is written down, LO-3 for what the term means. V53 gives the same Ar/Ca pair without the notation and gets LO-3 alone.

The octet rule is stated in terms of valence electrons (LO-3) and then applied to helium's 2 and neon's 2,8, which have to be built (LO-2). Fuller than V46, which asks only what eight electrons signify. As at V46, the inertness conclusion itself is stated by no outcome.

Both halves sit inside LO-3: what valence electrons are, and how their count fixes lose-gain-share, i.e. valency. This is the clearest case of LO-3's six-term row swallowing two questions that a finer curriculum would separate (compare V44 and V45, which ask the two halves singly and get the same code).

The shells have to be counted to 2,8,7 and turned into an identification of chlorine - LO-5's 'interpret data ... to classify elements accurately' - before valency 1 and the electron-gain route follow from LO-3. O21 reads a diagram too but stops at valency and never names the element, so it gets LO-2 and LO-3 instead.

POOR FIT, and the strongest of the three historical-sequence items (with N5 and O13) because it asks what each model IMPROVED - which is CG7's 'Science is ever evolving' almost verbatim. Still no learning outcome states the development of atomic models; C1.1 is cited as the one intact row naming Bohr's model.

A 3:1 abundance has to be turned into 75/25 and weighted (LO-5's 'interpret data, such as atomic mass') over LO-3's 'atomic mass' and 'isotopes'. Same mapping as P18 and S67. The closing ask - what the fractional value implies about any single atom - is covered by no outcome at all.

First half is the p = e neutrality and then the charge imbalance left by removing one electron - LO-1. Second half specifies that the electron removed is a VALENCE electron, which is LO-3. Not LO-4: nothing is counted, the question is about which balance holds.

The graded contrast is C-14 against C-12 - same protons, different neutrons - which is LO-3's isotope clause, and the drawing of the shells is LO-2. LO-4 is not cited because the neutron counts come with the isotope names rather than being computed from A and Z.

Exactly the two halves that V40 and V39 ask separately: what nucleons are, i.e. two particles identified by their position in the nucleus (LO-1), and A = p + n, the relation LO-4 is built on. Citing both is what distinguishes this item from either of those.

Three real strands, so three codes: the superscript/subscript layout is the international convention (LO-6), A = 15 + 16 = 31 has to be produced (LO-4), and the symbol P itself has to be supplied (C-1.3-LO-2, the reconstructed 'chemical symbols ... for the first eighteen elements according to IUPAC'). P13 and N11 only READ this notation; this item has to write it.

Isotopes, isobars, atomic number, mass number and the chemical-properties consequence - five of LO-3's six listed terms in one item, and one code covers all of it. The clearest demonstration that LO-3 cannot discriminate within this chapter; I am not going to split it artificially with LO-5, since no data are supplied, only recalled examples.

PARTIAL FIT, the mass gap again. The justification is that protons and neutrons are heavy and inside the nucleus while electrons are light and outside - the position half is LO-1's, the mass half is in no outcome. Same limitation as V35 and S70.

PARTIAL FIT, and a concrete cost of the LO-28 defect: 'draw a diagram ... according to Bohr's model' is the second item in the chapter that asks for a labelled model diagram, but LO-28's surviving text stops at 'Thomson's model, Rutherford's model and' - Bohr's model is in the truncated tail, so unlike S57 there is nothing to cite. LO-2 carries the energy levels drawn, C1.1 names Bohr's model.

PARTIAL FIT. The long-form twin of N10 and mapped identically on purpose: (a) the instability defect and (b) Bohr's stationary states, of which only the discrete-energy-level idea is reachable, through LO-2. No CG7 here even though (a) is a limitation, because (b) makes the physics the graded content - V31, which asks (a) alone, does get CG7.

(a) is discovery apparatus, which no outcome covers - note the diagram asked for is the cathode-ray TUBE, not an atomic model, so LO-28 does not apply even on its diagram clause. (b) is that the atom is divisible after all, which is V26's supersession point, hence CG7; LO-1 carries the electron's negative charge.

Every sub-question is a charge-or-position claim: which model predicted small deflections, what the straight-through majority implies about empty space, what the rebound implies about a dense centre. LO-1 throughout, with no shells, numbers or conventions in play.

The watermelon narrative resolves to the same three things as O10 and P2 - whose model, what the pulp and seeds stand for, and why the charges cancel. LO-1's charge and position clauses, honestly shared with the rest of the Thomson-analogy family; no legal code separates a story-framed version from a plain one.

(a) names the experiment and (c) draws the empty-space and dense-nucleus conclusions, which is LO-1. (b) asks what an alpha particle is - the O15 gap, covered by no outcome - so LO-1 is cited on the two parts it genuinely fits.

(a) is LO-1 word for word: the three particles and their relative charges. (b) the neutron's discovery history and (c) the neutron-to-proton ratio in heavy nuclei are both outside curriculum 82 entirely, so I cite LO-1 only and record the two gaps rather than stretching a code over them.

(a) is LO-5's 'maximum number of electrons in a shell' stated as the Bohr-Bury rules, while (b) and (c) are LO-2's distribution, written as 2,8,6 and then drawn. Same pair as O5, V41, V42 and S62; this item is simply the fullest version of it.

Valency plus the octet rule (LO-3) applied to configurations 2,6 and 2,8,2 that must be built first (LO-2). Mapped the same as S63, which is the same task on sodium and oxygen - a family that honestly shares one pair of outcomes.

(a) and (b) are squarely LO-3 - isobars defined, then contrasted with isotopes on Z and A. (c) asks for three medical or industrial applications, which is the V49 and S68 hole, so CG5 is cited alongside. This is the only item where the applications gap sits next to real outcome content instead of standing alone.
